documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Stoodio

documents.t: Stoodio's pitch is that it builds a brand's AI studio, and it is refreshingly specific about being fashion-only rather than a general image tool. The platform lists five integrated capabilities: image generation, video generation, workflows that chain prompts, models, edits, and exports into repeatable pipelines, a model database, and asset management. The model database is the strategy. As an official partner of ModelManagement.com, Stoodio offers access to over 100,000 consented digital twins with worldwide, perpetual commercial rights, and it is pointed about what that means—no composite faces, no grey zones. For a brand whose legal team is uneasy about synthetic likeness, or that operates in a market tightening around AI disclosure and personality rights, this is a materially different proposition from a library of invented faces. The company frames itself as a production partner rather than a tool, promising guided onboarding so a team integrates AI into real production from the first session. Its published evidence is a single detailed case study: a Berlin activewear brand reporting 40% lower cost per SKU, production cycles moving from three weeks to three days, and double the content output. There is no published pricing; the route in is a booked demo.
documents.s: Stoodio: licensing as the product strategy

documents.t: Astria shares Stoodio's fashion focus and diverges on autonomy and breadth. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit the brand's own people edit and run. Breadth shows in two places. Categories: templates treat beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct fashion disciplines, not variations on apparel. And casting: alongside adult models across body types, the library covers children's and extended-size casting, which are production requirements a licensed adult-model roster does not address.

documents.t: Stoodio's case study is genuinely useful—specific numbers, a named founder, a real brand—and it is one story from a small brand. That is honest early-stage evidence, and a buyer should read it as such rather than as a pattern. Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them: Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. documents.t: Consider a European brand whose counsel has flagged AI-generated faces as a risk. The marketing director wants AI production; legal wants documented consent and clear commercial rights for any human likeness used in advertising. This is Stoodio's scenario, and it answers it well. A licensed twin from a consented roster with worldwide perpetual rights is a document legal can read, and the onboarding engagement means someone from the vendor helps wire it into the brand's real production. If that constraint is genuinely binding, the rest of this comparison is secondary. Now change one detail: the brand also sells a children's line and a small jewelry capsule, and its campaign imagery is set by a freelance stylist who is not an employee. The licensed adult-model roster does not cover the children's line. Jewelry needs different lighting and macro conventions than activewear. And the stylist needs to be inside the workflow, reviewing looks with the team, not briefing a vendor. In Astria those are ordinary: children's and extended-size casting exist in the library, jewelry and beauty are first-class template categories, and the stylist joins the brand workspace and reviews on the multiplayer Board with live voice.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Stylic

documents.t: Stylic's promise is speed and price. The published workflow is three steps: upload a product image in any format, spend about a minute choosing from 500+ backgrounds and 30+ AI models, and download commercial-ready results roughly ninety seconds later. Features include single, multiple, and catalogue photoshoots, 4K and 8K output, brand watermarking, clothing colour change, custom AI models, and bulk creation. Plans run from around $23 to $58 a month with an enterprise option. The intended audience is stated plainly: Shopify stores, Amazon sellers, Meesho brands, D2C fashion labels, fashion startups, and creative agencies. The pricing, the marketplace orientation, and the rupee-denominated savings figure all point the same way—this is a tool for sellers, not a system for brands. The published statistics deserve a sceptical read. Stylic cites 10,000+ fashion businesses in one place and 200+ fashion brands in another, alongside 2.4 million images generated, a rupee figure for photoshoot budget saved, and a claim that 94% of users replaced their photographer. No methodology accompanies any of them, and the two audience-size figures are hard to reconcile. None of this means the product is bad; it means a buyer should ask how each number was produced before treating it as evidence, and should weigh it against a company profile that is early-stage and light on named references.
documents.s: Stylic: three minutes to a listing image

documents.t: Astria's buyer list includes the people Stylic's headline claim positions against. Photographers, studios, and educators use Astria to install repeatable production workflows for brands—which is a useful signal about what the product is for. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is stored and reused rather than reconfigured per shoot. Templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct categories, casting covers ages and body types including children and extended sizes, and the same direction extends into campaign frames, social crops, and motion.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Stylic's evidence is aggregate and self-reported: user counts, images generated, savings, and a replacement statistic, with marketplace names such as Myntra and Flipkart mentioned as context rather than as customers with published stories. Astria's public materials name fashion brands—Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, Nine West—alongside studios and photographers running client work. Vendor-published too, and checkable in a different way: a named brand can be looked at, and a photographer can be asked.
documents.s: Public proof: numbers versus names

documents.t: Consider a label that started on marketplaces and is now launching its own site, with 70 styles, a stylist on retainer, and a founder who cares how the clothes are framed. The Stylic era made sense: cheap listing images, generated fast, good enough for a marketplace grid where every competitor's photo looks similar. What breaks is not image quality—it is everything around it. The stylist's point of view cannot be stored, so each shoot is reconfigured from menus and drifts. The site needs a lookbook and campaign imagery, which the tool is not aimed at. Motion is not on offer. And when the founder asks for a warmer, tighter crop across all 70 styles, that is 70 reconfigurations rather than one edit. With Astria, the stylist sets casting, styling, lighting, crop, and format once, the founder approves it, and the 70 styles run against that treatment imported from Shopify or Google Drive. The lookbook and campaign come from the same direction. The crop change is a single edit applied everywhere. And the stylist's judgment is now an asset the brand keeps.
documents.s: A realistic workflow comparison: the seller who becomes a brand

documents.t: This is Stylic's genuine edge and the one concession that matters here. About three minutes from upload to download, with no setup and nothing to configure beyond two menus, is a genuinely low barrier — and for a seller listing a handful of products it may be all that is required. No production system competes with that on immediacy, and there is nothing wrong with buying the simple thing when the simple thing is sufficient.
documents.s: Time to first image — winner: Stylic

documents.t: Stylic's headline statistic frames AI as a substitute for a professional. Astria's position is the opposite, and it is not merely rhetorical: photographers and studios are among Astria's users because the product lets them encode a look and hand it to a brand's team to run. That is the difference between removing craft from the process and making craft repeatable. Brands that have paid for good creative direction generally want to keep it.

documents.t: Tellos positions itself as an AI fashion video and photo studio for ecommerce brands, with a blunt promise: no studios, no models, no production chaos. Upload flat-lay or mannequin shots, generate on-model images and video, and publish. Output is optimized for Shopify product pages, Instagram Reels, TikTok, and Meta Ads, and the Shopify integration is a few clicks rather than an engineering task. Two capabilities stand out. Tellos advertises private AI models trained on a brand's style, fits, and visual language, which is a serious answer to consistency rather than a menu of presets. And its heritage in shoppable video shows: the company sells a storefront video layer priced by monthly traffic, separate from its generation studio. That heritage also produces its best evidence. Tellos publishes a customer story with Inglot reporting a 17% conversion-rate uplift and an 11% increase in average order value from shoppable video on the storefront. It is vendor-written and specific to that brand's implementation, but it is a commerce outcome rather than a production-speed claim, which makes it more useful than most case studies in this category.
documents.s: Tellos: video-first content for the storefront

documents.t: Astria's unit of work is the treatment rather than the asset. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live together in a brand workspace, so an approved look becomes something the team runs repeatedly instead of something one operator recreates each time. That shows up in coverage. Templates span beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial work, not only standard apparel PDPs. Brand references keep results anchored to the brand rather than a generic AI aesthetic, and Astria's Describe tool can extract usable creative direction from a rights-cleared reference while accounting for the products and models already loaded. Motion is an extension of the same workspace: a still the brand has already approved can be animated with a choice of current video options, so the campaign's casting and styling survive into the clip.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Tellos names brands including INGLOT, Crocs, Sereia, and Strongful, and its Inglot story quantifies storefront impact. This is first-party evidence, and it is strongest where Tellos is strongest: content that lives on a product page and moves a conversion metric. Astria's public materials show a production base among brands and the professionals who create for them, including Ronny Kobo, Gant, Lee Cooper, and Nine West, alongside studios and photographers running client work. Also vendor-published, and also an adoption signal rather than a quality proof. The two point at different rooms in the same building: Tellos at the storefront, Astria at the studio that feeds it.
documents.s: Public proof: commerce outcomes versus production adoption

documents.t: Consider a footwear brand launching 40 styles. Each needs PDP stills, a detail shot, a short clip for the product page, paid-social cutdowns, and a campaign image for the seasonal landing page. Two colorways arrive late. With Tellos, the team uploads product shots and generates on-model stills and clips, then publishes them to Shopify and social with formats already sized per channel. For the video job specifically this is efficient, and the storefront layer means the clips are not just assets but merchandising. What the workflow does not carry is the creative decision. The campaign image, the lookbook treatment, and the late colorways each start again from generation choices, and the brand's visual language lives in a trained model plus whatever the operator remembers. With Astria, the team establishes casting, styling, lighting, crop, and format once and approves it. The 40 styles run against that treatment; the late colorways inherit it; the campaign image and the social crops are extensions of the same direction rather than separate jobs. When the clip is generated, it animates a still the brand already signed off, which is why the motion looks like the campaign instead of adjacent to it.

documents.t: Tellos's brand-trained models are a genuine consistency mechanism, and they deserve more credit than a preset menu. But a trained model captures a look, not a process. It cannot tell the next operator that this brand crops footwear tight at the ankle, casts older than the category, and never shoots on a white sweep. Astria encodes those decisions as a reusable treatment, which is what makes an approved direction survive a new hire, a new agency, or a new season.

A video layer that installs on Shopify, plays on the product page, and comes with a published conversion outcome is a merchandising capability, not just an asset pipeline. Astria produces the video; it does not sell the storefront surface that plays it. Brands whose actual goal is on-site video merchandising should evaluate Tellos on that basis—and note that it is priced by traffic tier, which is a different commercial shape from paying for production.

For a PDP loop that distinction rarely matters. For a campaign where the film and the stills must read as one shoot, it decides whether the work holds together.

documents.s: Quick verdict: Astria vs Tolstoy

documents.t: Tolstoy's pitch is a sequence: create AI product content, make it shoppable, help shoppers choose. AI Studio generates on-brand product images and video from photos and brand guidelines. AI Player publishes shoppable video, galleries, and interactive widgets on the storefront. AI Shopper is an assistant offering recommendations, catalog guidance, and try-on. The platform is Shopify-native and widely adopted—the company cites over 5,000 Shopify brands—and it publishes commerce outcomes such as a 24% conversion lift at LSKD and a 15% AOV lift at Pantynova. Named customers include Culture Kings, Hampden, Skin Rocks, Laura Mercier, The Ordinary, Milk Makeup, Tarte, and KitchenAid. That customer list is the most informative thing on the site. Tolstoy is a general ecommerce content and merchandising platform that fashion brands use, not a fashion platform. Skincare, cosmetics, and kitchen appliances have real content needs, and a system designed to serve all of them well is necessarily designed around what they share—a product, a page, a shopper—rather than around casting, drape, fit, and collection logic.
documents.s: Tolstoy: three products around the product page

documents.t: Astria narrows deliberately. Products, casting, references, templates, and outputs live in a brand workspace, and the approved treatment—casting, styling, scene, crop, lighting, format—is the reusable unit that produces the season. The narrowing is what buys the depth. Templates cover apparel, beauty, jewelry, footwear, sports, luxury, and editorial as distinct fashion categories rather than as generic product photography. The casting library spans ages and body types, including children and extended-size casting. Campaign frames, editorial spreads, social crops, and motion all derive from the same approved direction, and review happens on a multiplayer Board where the photographer, the in-house studio, and the agency work on the same canvas.
documents.s: Astria: a professional fashion-production environment

documents.t: Tolstoy's evidence is strong for what it sells: named brands, a large Shopify install base, and specific conversion and AOV figures. It is vendor-published and concentrated on merchandising outcomes rather than production quality, which is the right emphasis for a commerce platform. Astria's public materials show a production base among fashion brands and the professionals who create for them—Ronny Kobo, Nununu, Gant, Lee Cooper, Nine West—alongside studios and photographers running client work. Also vendor-published. Tolstoy proves that its widgets sell product; Astria's evidence is about who produces fashion imagery with it.

documents.t: Consider a fashion brand on Shopify with 400 SKUs and a two-person ecommerce team. It needs four PDP images per SKU, a lookbook, campaign assets, and social content, and it is attracted to buying one platform instead of three. The bundle logic is genuinely appealing until the arithmetic. 400 SKUs at four images is 1,600 images. Tolstoy's highest published AI Studio tier equates to roughly a thousand images a month, so the catalog alone exceeds the top self-serve tier before any rejected frame, colorway, or campaign asset. The player is metered separately by impressions with per-thousand overage, and the assistant by its own tokens. Three meters, three consumption curves, and a conversation with sales as soon as the catalog is real. The creative question matters more. Brand guidelines are an input Tolstoy consumes per asset; they are not the same as an approved treatment that fixes casting, crop, and styling across a collection. The lookbook and campaign work is outside what the content module is aimed at, so it still needs an answer. With Astria, the 400 SKUs import from Shopify and run against one approved treatment. The lookbook and campaign extend that direction rather than starting over, motion animates approved stills, and pricing is scoped to what the brand creates rather than to three separate meters. If the brand also wants a shoppable player and an AI assistant on the storefront, those remain available to buy—from Tolstoy or anyone else—without conflating them with production.

documents.t: A platform serving apparel, skincare, and small appliances optimizes for the common denominator. Fashion's hard parts—drape on a sheer fabric, casting that matches a brand's customer, a crop convention the brand has used for six seasons—are not common-denominator problems. Astria is narrower on purpose, and that is where the depth comes from.

The first produces assets that are roughly on-brand and individually variable; the second produces a collection that is consistent because consistency is the stored object, not an instruction repeated per asset.

documents.t: Tolstoy's content focus is the storefront. A season also needs a lookbook, campaign frames, editorial treatments, and social-native crops, and those are not storefront assets. documents.t: Three metered products with separate allowances make a collection hard to plan and easy to over-run: content tokens for images and video, impressions with overage for the player, tokens again for the assistant. Astria treats the collection as the unit of work and prices to usage—pay for what you create. This article makes no claim that Astria is cheaper; it observes that a bundle discount across three meters is not a production budget. documents.t: For fashion brands, Astria is the stronger choice: it is built for how a collection is produced rather than for how a product page is merchandised. Tolstoy is a capable commerce platform, and its content module is a convenience within that platform rather than a reason to choose it over a production system. The two are not mutually exclusive. Just do not let a bundle discount decide how your collection gets made.

documents.t: Count your real annual volume first: SKUs times images, plus colorways, plus campaign and social assets, plus a realistic rejection rate. Check that number against the token allowances of any metered plan before you shortlist. Then run five representative SKUs through both, require PDP, detail, campaign, and social crops, and add a colorway after approval. Have a senior creative review outputs blind for garment fidelity, drape, anatomy, styling, and brand fit. Finally, ask a second operator to reproduce the approved direction from scratch.

documents.t: Start with five representative garments and produce the required product views. Approve those against the references, then ask for a campaign frame with different lighting and a wider composition. Keep the casting and garment fixed while the scene changes. This is the revealing test. It exposes whether creative direction can change without altering a hem, fastening, print scale, or face. Repeat with a layered look and then a new colourway. Record the rejected attempts and any manual correction; do not count only the successful final click. Have the person who normally reviews your brand's imagery approve the results without platform labels. Then give the saved work to a colleague and ask them to extend it. A repeatable workflow should survive that handoff. Read consistent AI fashion models for a focused casting test.

documents.s: The shortlist by job

documents.t: Astria is the most direct option here for a fashion team that has a flat-lay product photo and needs the product to move. The Astria 3D ghost packshot workflow returns one six-second 1080p MP4 rotation plus front, side, and three-quarter stills. The assets are designed for product pages, Reels, TikTok, and ad creative. The operational difference is substantial: no turntable, model, studio booking, or sample shipment. Choose a locked template for the product class, upload the flat lay, and use the resulting rotation and stills across the collection. Astria’s page currently describes pay-per-SKU use with no subscription and advertises entry pricing “from $9”; those are Astria-reported product and pricing claims, current on the review date, and may change. The trade-off is equally important. Astria infers views that the one input photograph does not show. The output is a generated video, not a photographed sequence and not a model containing geometry, materials, or verified dimensions. Review prints, logos, closures, hardware, hemlines, back construction, and product color against the real SKU before publication. Choose Astria when: the product is fashion, speed and no-shipping production matter, an MP4 rotation answers the channel need, and your team can approve the inferred views. Start with one difficult SKU before scaling highly structured or sheer products. Do not choose Astria for this job when: the shopper must freely control the camera, the deliverable must be GLB or USDZ, AR scale must be dimensionally validated, or a marketplace and product-risk policy requires calibrated physical evidence.
documents.s: 1. Astria: the fast fashion rotation from one flat lay

documents.t: GoPackshot is the closest match for a buyer who means, “Take our products and return ecommerce-ready assets.” Its services page describes packshot, model, ghost-mannequin and flat-lay photography; video and 360-degree content; product logistics; retouching; quality control; and delivery into brand systems. The important word is managed. You ship physical inventory and buy an operating service, not a self-serve 3D application. That makes GoPackshot a credible choice when color, garment construction, marketplace rules, product handling, and accountability matter more than owning the capture line. GoPackshot also publishes claims about color tolerances, daily capacity, studio count, integrations, and tracked logistics. Treat those as vendor-reported claims, then put the relevant ones into the contract or test brief. A public capacity number does not establish capacity for your garment mix, revision policy, or launch window. Its public service description includes 360-degree video, but does not describe the output as a freely navigable GLB or USDZ model. If you need true 3D, ask three blunt questions: Is the deliverable an image sequence, video, web viewer, or model file? Can the shopper move to an angle that was never photographed? Do we receive geometry, materials, dimensions, and usage rights? If the answers are “sequence,” “no,” and “no,” you are buying a photographic spin. That can be an excellent asset. It is not a true 3D model.
documents.s: 2. GoPackshot: managed physical production

documents.t: Orbitvu sells automated photography systems rather than operating as your outsourced packshot studio. Its ecommerce product line covers stills, 360-degree images and video; its fashion positioning includes ghost mannequin, flat lay, on-figure work, and standardized footwear angles. This route changes the economics. Instead of paying a service per project or SKU, you own equipment, studio utilization, operators, styling, color management, maintenance, and workflow integration. The best candidate already has products moving through one facility and a team that can keep a capture recipe stable. Vendor language such as “web-ready content in minutes” is vendor-reported and should be separated into capture time, operator touch time, retouching time, rework, and publishing time. A fast turntable does not dress a mannequin, correct a crushed collar, approve color, or resolve a barcode mismatch. Choose Orbitvu when the problem is repeatable physical capture at sustained volume. Do not choose it because the word “360” appears near “3D.” Confirm the exact output your selected system produces.
documents.s: 3. Orbitvu: bring automated capture in-house

documents.t: PhotoRobot also sells hardware and workflow software for in-house or studio operators. Its public output gallery explicitly separates still images, 360 spins, “3D spins,” photogrammetry 3D models, and 360 video. That taxonomy is useful because it exposes how different outputs are often grouped under one marketing label. For fashion, PhotoRobot sells ghost-mannequin equipment and describes workflows for stills, spins, and ecommerce 3D models. Those are vendor-reported capabilities. Ask to see an output from the same product class and material as yours: a matte sneaker is not evidence for patent leather; a rigid bag is not evidence for a soft dress. PhotoRobot is the more relevant shortlist entry when you want a configurable automated studio and may need several capture modes. The procurement risk is complexity: a system that can produce five asset types still needs five acceptance standards.
documents.s: 4. PhotoRobot: automated capture with a wider output menu

documents.t: Threekit belongs in the shortlist only when the buying problem is interactive 3D rather than photography. Its platform overview distinguishes virtual photography, WebGL-based interactive 3D, and augmented reality. Its platform can create glTF and USDZ variants for web AR and supports configurable products whose visual state changes with selected options. That is a materially different deliverable. The shopper can interact with geometry and materials, and the same product definition can support many configurations. It is especially relevant to customizable bags, footwear, jewelry, furniture, equipment, or other structured products where options and spatial understanding affect purchase. The hard part is the asset system behind the viewer. Before buying, scope who creates the base geometry, materials, variant logic, dimensions, and future revisions. Threekit publishes commercial performance statistics; treat every such number as a vendor-reported result, not a forecast for your store. For a single non-configurable garment, this can be more system than the buying question deserves. For a configurable product family, it may be the only category here that actually solves the problem.
documents.s: 5. Threekit: true 3D, configuration, and AR

documents.t: VNTANA is best understood as a 3D asset pipeline. Its 3D commerce page describes taking existing CAD or 3D files, optimizing them, and distributing web-ready 3D and AR assets to commerce channels. That is valuable when product development already produces usable 3D assets. It is not the same as shipping a garment to a photography studio. Ask whether model creation or cleanup is included in your scope, because “upload your 3D file” assumes the most expensive input may already exist. VNTANA publishes performance claims for 3D commerce; those are vendor-reported. Evaluate the platform on file reduction, visual fidelity after optimization, variant handling, viewer performance, publishing integrations, and the labor saved in your actual catalog.
documents.s: 6. VNTANA: optimize and distribute models you already have

documents.t: For a Shopify merchant with a small, prioritized model list, the most direct procurement path may be a 3D-modeling partner rather than an enterprise platform. Shopify’s partner guidance says a modeler may need multi-angle photographs, dimensions in millimeters, diagrams, and CAD files where available. It also provides a practical review checklist for shape, scale, materials, reflections, textures, edges, and unwanted gaps. Shopify says the delivered model should be a GLB, approximately 4 MB and no more than 15 MB under the guidance on that page. Recheck current limits before commissioning because platform requirements change. Your theme must also support the media type; see the Shopify product media guide before approving the project. This route is strong when true 3D is needed for ten important products, not ten thousand speculative ones.
documents.s: 7. Shopify Partners: bounded custom model production

documents.t: Do not ask each supplier for “a 3D packshot quote.” Send one matrix and require every cell to be answered. Score published assets, not sales demos.

documents.t: Astria should be scored on the asset it actually delivers: a fast AI-generated rotation video and angle stills from one fashion flat lay. It should not be scored as a true 3D modeling bureau. The strongest hybrid uses an approved packshot or well-lit flat lay as Astria’s input, reviews the inferred views against the physical SKU, and publishes the MP4 where rotation communicates shape or drape. Keep calibrated photography for exact color and construction evidence. Buy true 3D only when arbitrary viewing, configuration, or AR is the requirement. That gives Astria a clear place in the buying decision rather than pretending every “3D packshot” is the same file. For the full format distinction, read 3D packshots for ecommerce. For the physical-to-generative operating handoff, continue to AI product photography vs a packshot studio.

Choose Astria for a fast AI-generated fashion rotation video and angle stills from one flat lay, a managed studio for approved physical photography and captured spins, capture equipment for a repeatable in-house studio, a model-creation partner for a true GLB or USDZ, and a 3D commerce platform for configuration, AR, or multi-channel delivery.

Its 3D ghost packshot workflow takes one flat-lay photo and returns a six-second 1080p rotation video plus three angle stills for social and product pages. It does not return an interactive GLB or USDZ model, and inferred views still require product-accuracy review.

documents.t: GoPackshot's public services page describes packshot photography, ghost mannequin, video, and 360-degree content within a managed physical production service. It does not present those outputs as freely navigable GLB or USDZ models. Ask for the exact deliverable, viewer, and file format rather than assuming that 360 means true 3D.
documents.s: Does GoPackshot create true interactive 3D models?

documents.t: No. A photographic 360 spin is a sequence of captured angles. A true 3D model contains geometry and materials, can usually be viewed from arbitrary angles, and may support augmented reality. Some vendors use the word “3D” for a spin effect, so inspect the exported file and interaction rather than the label.
documents.s: Is a 360 spin the same as a 3D product model?

documents.t: Buy equipment when physical products already flow through one location, the shot recipe is stable, utilization will be high, and the team can own styling, color management, maintenance, and quality control. Outsource when volume is irregular or operational ownership would sit with nobody.
documents.s: When should a brand buy automated 360 capture equipment?

documents.t: Look at an AI-produced catalog that has gone wrong and you will usually find the same failure: it is not one model wearing forty garments, it is forty slightly different people. If your model is specified in words, you are recasting on every generation. documents.t: "A woman in her late twenties, shoulder-length brown hair, olive skin, natural makeup" feels specific. It is not. It describes a category that contains an enormous number of distinct faces, and each generation is free to choose a different one. Add more adjectives and you narrow the category slightly; you never reduce it to a person. This is why prompt-only workflows produce a type rather than a model. The images are consistent in the way that stock photography is consistent — same genre, different humans. The fix is categorical rather than incremental: the likeness has to exist as a stored thing that gets pointed at, not a description that gets re-interpreted. Once a face is a reference the production can reuse, "the same model" becomes a fact about the setup rather than a hope about the output.
documents.s: Why description fails

documents.t: Teams say "consistency" and mean different things. All four are needed, and they fail independently. Identity consistency — the same recognisable person. This is what references solve. Styling consistency — hair and makeup that stay the same. A stored likeness will happily give you the same face with a different fringe. Hair, in particular, drifts more than faces do and is worth calling out explicitly in the direction. Treatment consistency — same light, same grade, same lens character, same background logic. Independent of who the person is. Framing consistency — crops and proportions that match across the set. A catalog can fail on any one of these while passing the other three, and the symptom looks similar to a non-specialist: "it looks off." Diagnosing which of the four broke is the first step in fixing it.
documents.s: Four kinds of consistency, often confused

documents.t: Store the likeness, don't describe it. Whether via a trained model from eight to sixteen varied photos or an instant reference from fewer, the point is the same: the identity becomes an asset in the production rather than a sentence in a prompt. Vary the source material. Reference images should span angles, lighting conditions, and expressions. Sixteen frames from one burst teach the system one lighting condition and one angle, and the likeness collapses the moment you ask for anything else. Separate the person from everything else. Casting, garment, pose, and scene should be independently specifiable. When they are entangled — one long prompt describing all four — changing the pose perturbs the face. This separation is the single biggest practical difference between tools that hold consistency and tools that do not. Lock the treatment before scaling. Approve light, grade, and framing on a handful of products first. Drift compounds; a slightly warm bias in the setup becomes visible warmth by image 200. Review as a set, never as singles. This is a process fix, not a technical one, and it catches more than any technical measure. Contact-sheet the whole run at a size where faces are legible. Re-anchor periodically. On long runs, check late images against the earliest approved ones rather than against the images immediately before them. Drift is a slow gradient; comparing neighbours will never reveal it.
documents.s: What actually works

documents.t: Seeds. Reusing a seed reproduces a similar result for a near-identical prompt. Change the pose, the garment, or the scene — which is the entire job — and the likeness moves. Useful for reproducibility, not for identity. Longer descriptions. Adding adjectives narrows the category but never collapses it to one person. Twenty-word casting descriptions are a symptom of the wrong approach, not a solution to it. Picking the best of many. Generating forty options and choosing the most similar is expensive, slow, and still drifts, because you are selecting from a distribution rather than fixing it. Face-swapping at the end. Pasting a consistent face onto inconsistent bodies produces a characteristic uncanny result: the head belongs to someone whose build, skin tone, and lighting do not match the body beneath it.
documents.s: What does not work

documents.t: One consequence worth stating: consistency work is what makes broad casting practical. If every image is a fresh roll of the dice, representing a range of ages, sizes, and bodies across a collection is unmanageable — you cannot hold six different people consistent when you cannot hold one. Once casting is a stored reference, a brand can run a genuinely varied cast — including children's ranges and extended sizing — with the same reliability as a single model. Whether a brand does that is a values question. Consistency is what turns it from an aspiration into an operation. For portraits of real employees, the challenge is different: preserve each person while matching the photographic treatment across people. Use the AI team photos and headshots workflow for the submission brief and approval process.
documents.s: The extended-casting problem

documents.t: Before committing to a platform, run this: Establish one model. Produce ten images: five garments, two poses each, one indoor scene and one outdoor. Contact-sheet them at a size where faces are clearly legible. Ask someone who has not seen them: "Is this one person or more than one?" Then change the scene to something quite different — night, harsh light, a different location — and repeat. Step five is where most tools fail. Consistency under similar conditions is common; consistency across genuinely different lighting is what a real collection demands. For the full production context, see the AI fashion photoshoot guide. For lookbooks specifically, where casting continuity carries the narrative, see the AI lookbook guide.

documents.t: Because a text description is not an identity. Words like "woman, 28, brown hair" describe a category containing millions of faces, and each generation picks a different one. Consistency requires the likeness to be stored as a reusable reference, not re-described each time.

documents.t: Only weakly. Reusing a seed reproduces similar results for a near-identical prompt, but the likeness drifts as soon as the pose, scene, or framing changes — which is exactly what a collection requires. Seeds are a reproducibility tool, not an identity tool.

documents.t: For a trained likeness, typically eight to sixteen varied images. Instant reference approaches can work from far fewer. Variety across angle, lighting, and expression matters more than volume in either case.

documents.t: The gradual change in a model's appearance across a long production run — subtly different face, age, or build between early and late images. It is rarely visible image-by-image and obvious when the set is viewed together.

You can now generate instant custom headshot photos for professional use in just a few clicks. Several industries could benefit from it. Here are some key ones: 1. Many companies request profile pictures for internal directories. 3. Events & Conferences: Attendees at conferences or trade shows might need quick headshots for badges or presentations. Event organizers may require speaker headshots for promotional materials. 4. Retail & Hospitality: Retailers or restaurants can use headshot generators for employee name tags or online staff directories. 5. Education & Training: Online courses or educational platforms can benefit from student profile pictures. Professional development programs often require headshots for certificates or online profiles. 6. Media & Marketing: Content creators or bloggers frequently need quick headshots for social media profiles or website bios. Marketing agencies can use headshot generators for clients who need profile pictures on short notice. So how do we at Astria.ai come in? With our FaceID tool, you can instantly fine-tune your images while preserving identity in a matter of seconds. All you need is just one photograph. This feature comes in very handy if you need to generate images quickly and efficiently – such as if you’re offering a free-tier service in a user app and need profile images to be generated in a jiffy. It can also be applied in real-time applications like live-streaming or virtual try-ons. In e-commerce applications, instant fine-tuning can be a game-changer as it allows users to visualize products with their own images seamlessly, enhancing the shopping experience and boosting conversion rates. In the gaming industry, instant fine-tuning can be used to create personalized gaming avatars or characters that resemble the user, thereby increasing immersion and emotional connection with the game. Additionally, social media platforms could use the FaceID feature to offer instant filters and lenses, letting users create and share more personalized content with their friends and followers. Just one point to remember: the adapter was trained on human faces, so best not to try faces of your pets or other subjects at the moment. A few other points to note: FaceID can work with Face Swap to improve similarity. Disable Face Swap in case your prompt is animation style. For fast generation, use LCM schedulers. For realistic images, enable Face-Correct to improve the facial features.
documents.s: FaceID: Studio-Quality Portraits Without Training a Model

documents.t: Astria offers full fine-tuning tools using the Dreambooth API. This is a technique that updates the entire Stable Diffusion model by training on just a few images of a subject or style. This is a pretty efficient way of fine-tuning as it allows for the generation of realistic and diverse images of the specific subjects or concepts. Apart from this, Astria also has the option of LoRA fine-tuning. In this technique, instead of fine-tuning the entire model, a low-rank adapter layer is inserted into the model architecture. This reduces the computational time and storage requirements leading to a lower cost of fine-tuning. Both the techniques above are well suited for high fidelity on identity preservation of the subject images, but they take around 5-10 minutes for process completion and, therefore, we have FaceID for instant results. FaceID does not involve training of the model at all. Under the hood it only calculates and retains the embeddings of the training images, and then reproduces these embeddings during inference. This way the Stable Diffusion model doesn’t have to go through any changes in its weights, and that’s why the fine-tuning process is so rapid. It takes less than 10 seconds for a FaceID based fine-tune to be created.
documents.s: FaceID vs Full Fine-Tuning

documents.t: As mentioned before, the FaceID fine-tune can be done with just one image. But, for the sake of fidelity, we’ve taken 3 images of a model from Unsplash. Here are the input images: Now head over to the New Finetune section. Under the Advanced features, select the Model type as FaceID. Remember to provide the Class name (woman, in this case). Your tune will be ready in a matter of seconds. Here’s the API to create the tune: curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_KEY" https://api.astria.ai/tunes \ -F tune[title]="Unsplash Model Female - 1" \ -F tune[name]=woman \ -F tune[base_tune_id]=690204 \ -F tune[images][0]="@1.jpg" \ -F tune[images][1]="@2.jpg" \ -F tune[images][2]="@3.jpg" \ Base_tune_id = 69024 refers to the Realistic Vision V5.1 (VAE) model that we used as the base model. You can check out the list of available models here. Let’s start prompting with some real-life use cases, where instant headshot generation would be useful.

documents.t: Every fashion shoot budget is assembled from the same components. Rates vary enormously by market — a day in London, New York, or Milan is not a day in a smaller city — so treat what follows as a structure to fill in rather than a price list. Photographer. Quoted as a day rate, sometimes with a separate creative fee for campaign work. The single most variable line: an experienced commercial photographer with a name commands a multiple of a competent working professional, and both may deliver what your brand needs. Assistants. Usually one or two, at a fraction of the photographer's rate. Non-optional on anything with real lighting. Model. Booked through an agency, at a day rate plus agency commission — commonly around 20% — plus usage. The usage line is the one that surprises people; see below. Hair and makeup. One artist for a single model; two if you are shooting several looks against the clock. Stylist. Day rate plus prep days, which are real and frequently forgotten. Pulling and returning samples takes as long as shooting them. Studio or location. A studio day, or a location fee plus permits, plus a scout day if the location is not already known. Equipment. Often included in the photographer's rate; specialist lighting, grip, or digital capture is not. Production. A producer, catering, transport, and shipping samples both ways. Small productions absorb this into someone's job. Large ones cannot. Post-production. Quoted per image, and this is where volume bites. Retouching 20 editorial images is a project; retouching 600 catalog variants is a different business entirely. Usage rights. Frequently the largest hidden line. Talent and location licensing is scoped by territory, media, and duration. Extending a campaign, or reusing an image in a market you did not license, means renegotiating — often at a worse rate, because you have already committed creatively.
documents.s: The line items

documents.t: Rather than invent precise figures, here is how the proportions typically fall — which is more useful for planning than any single number. Small ecommerce day. Photographer, one assistant, one model, one hair-and-makeup artist, studio, standard retouching. Crew is the majority of the cost; post scales with SKU count and often overtakes the shoot fee. Usage is usually limited and cheap. Lookbook. Adds a stylist with prep days, a location, and more considered post. Styling and location can rival the photographer's fee. Deliverable count is low, so cost per finished image is high — by design. Campaign. Adds a producer, a larger crew, casting with a recognisable face, and broad usage rights. Talent and usage frequently dominate everything else, and the shoot day becomes a minority of the budget. The consistent pattern: as ambition rises, the photography becomes a smaller share and the rights and people become a larger one.
documents.s: Three realistic shapes

documents.t: Reshoots. Something arrives late, a sample is wrong, the light was not there. Ask explicitly who pays. Sample logistics. Shipping a collection to a location, insured, and back again. Your own time. The hours your team spends briefing, attending, selecting, and revising are real cost. On small teams they are the largest uncounted line by a wide margin. The calendar. The most expensive item on this list and the one that never appears on an invoice: a product that cannot be listed for three weeks because the shoot is booked for the 14th. For a seasonal business that delay has a direct revenue number attached. Revision. Deciding after delivery that the grade should be warmer means a grading session, or a reshoot, or living with it. Most brands live with it, which is its own kind of cost.
documents.s: The costs nobody quotes

documents.t: The honest framing is not "cents versus thousands," though that comparison is technically accurate and endlessly repeated. Generation cost per image is genuinely a rounding error. The fully-loaded comparison has to include: Setup time to reach an approved creative direction — real, and typically a day or two Review cycles with whoever owns the brand Rejected variants, which nobody publishes but everybody produces Correction time on garments that do not convert cleanly The salaried hours of whoever runs the process Counted properly, the per-image gap narrows considerably. It remains large — but the more defensible arguments are structural rather than arithmetic: Scheduling disappears. No model availability, no studio booking, no sample shipping, no three-week wait. Revision becomes cheap. A change of mind after approval is an edit, not a reshoot. For most teams this is the biggest practical difference. The long tail becomes affordable. Products that could never justify a shoot day can be presented properly — which is where the revenue argument usually lives. Direction is retained. The approved treatment is reusable next season rather than expiring with the shoot. The side-by-side model is worked through in AI versus traditional photoshoot cost, and the per-variant view in product photography cost per SKU. For a figure against your own catalog rather than a worked example, the photoshoot calculator counts the products in your store that need imagery and prices the coverage from there.
documents.s: How the AI comparison actually works

documents.t: Ask every supplier the same six questions: What is included — crew, studio, equipment, catering, transport? How many finished, retouched images, and to what standard? What usage rights, for which territories, media, and duration? What happens if we need a reshoot, and who pays? What is the revision policy after delivery? What do we own at the end — final files only, or raws and layered files too? Question three is where most budget overruns originate. Question five is where most disappointment does.
documents.s: How to compare two quotes properly

documents.t: A single-day commercial fashion shoot commonly lands somewhere between a few thousand and several tens of thousands, depending on crew size, location, talent, and usage rights. The range is wide because "photoshoot" describes anything from one photographer in a rented studio to a full production unit.
documents.s: How much does a fashion photoshoot cost?

documents.t: Usually post-production and usage rights. Retouching is quoted per image and scales with volume, and licensing for a model or location often costs more over time than the shoot day itself — particularly when a campaign is extended or reused.
documents.s: What is the biggest hidden cost in a photoshoot?

documents.t: Because quotes bundle different things. One may include retouching, licensing, and a producer; another may cover the shoot day alone. Compare quotes line by line, and specifically check usage rights, retouching volume, and who pays for reshoots.
documents.s: Why do photoshoot quotes vary so much?

documents.t: Highly variable, but a well-run ecommerce day produces far more usable frames than an editorial day, because the setup is fixed. Editorial days may yield only a handful of finished images. Always agree deliverable counts rather than shooting hours.
documents.s: How many images does a shoot day produce?

documents.t: Per image, dramatically. Fully loaded, the gap is smaller than headline figures suggest once setup, review, rejected variants, and staff time are counted. The larger practical saving is usually the removal of scheduling and sample logistics rather than the per-image price. Price your catalog with the photoshoot calculator, or explore Astria for fashion and ecommerce.
documents.s: Is AI photography cheaper than a photoshoot?

documents.t: A fashion video ad has to earn attention, identify the product, and give the viewer a reason to visit a matching page. A beautiful campaign cut can do the first job while leaving the other two unfinished. Start with one product proposition and two opening hooks. Keep the evidence, offer, destination, and closing action the same. This gives the production team a small deliverable and the marketing team a question it can actually test. Timings and creative structures below are suggested briefs, not platform rules or promised performance results.

documents.t: A campaign film builds a world. A product-page demonstration helps someone inspect an item. An acquisition ad has to connect an interruption in a feed with a useful next step. Write that connection in one sentence before choosing footage: “Show the jacket's removable collar, then take interested shoppers to that jacket.” The AI fashion film guide covers the broader motion production. Here the unit of work is an ad variant with a defined hypothesis. If your main need is a faithful demonstration for an existing shopper, start with apparel product-video production. A complete brief names the audience, product or collection, proposition, evidence, destination, placement, offer, and primary success metric. An ad for a single jacket should land where that jacket is immediately identifiable. If the selected color is unavailable, fix the brief or destination before producing more variants.
documents.s: Give acquisition creative its own brief

documents.t: Collect an approved hero frame, an accurate detail view, any real demonstration footage, product names, current offer copy, and the destination URL. Store the SKU and colorway with each visual. Add the approved logo, type treatment, audio permissions, and final copy as separate editing assets. Astria's ecommerce workflow describes creating imagery from product inputs and creative templates. Those reviewed stills can form the visual source kit for an ad. They still need product approval before they become motion, and the final cut needs editing, audio, and placement review. Use generated scenes to explore framing or extend an approved visual treatment. Use real product footage when the ad claims something demonstrable, such as a detachable part or pocket capacity. Keep text, prices, and end cards in the edit so a commercial revision does not require regenerating the garment. Record what is permitted for the assets you use, including paid advertising and the planned channels. For a creator-led ad, obtain the creator's agreed usage scope; do not turn a synthetic presenter into an invented customer testimonial. These are production checks, not a substitute for reviewing the applicable platform and campaign requirements.
documents.s: Build a small source kit

documents.t: Consider a jacket with a genuinely removable collar. The following brief is illustrative: confirm the product feature before using this copy. The timing is an editing target, not a claim about the ideal length of every fashion ad. Time Visual Job 0–3 seconds Hook A: full jacket with collar; Hook B: close-up of collar being removed Test product-first versus detail-first opening 3–8 seconds The same filmed removal and reattachment demonstration in both versions Establish that the feature is real 8–12 seconds Two approved styling views of the exact jacket Show how the feature changes the look 12–15 seconds Stable jacket hero and edited “Shop the jacket” end card Give a clear next step matching the destination Keep the audio, text treatment, total duration, and all footage after the opening the same across A and B. If you change the first image and the opening copy together, call the test an opening-package test. It cannot isolate which of those two changes drove the result. Design speech and music deliberately, but make product identity and the action understandable with sound off. Caption speech that carries the proposition. Watch the actual export on a phone: a neat desktop layout can still make a product name or fastening too small to see.
documents.s: A 15-second edit with a clear job for each beat

documents.t: Generating three hooks, four offers, three avatars, and two soundtracks creates 72 combinations before any evidence tells you which variation matters. It also spreads review effort and media spend across many different questions. For the first test, produce two exports of the same proposition: Element Version A Version B Opening Full product in the first frame Feature detail in the first frame Demonstration Same approved footage Same approved footage Offer and CTA Same wording Same wording Landing page Same product destination Same product destination Audience and delivery settings Held steady within the test Held steady within the test TikTok's split-testing documentation describes separating the audience into exclusive groups for a controlled comparison. Its testing-variable guide lists creative assets, including opening hooks, and permits one selected variable per split test. Check compatibility with your objective and campaign setup before promising a particular experiment. Use the platform's experiment tool when available. Two ads placed in an ordinary optimized ad group are not automatically a balanced experiment: unequal delivery can reflect the delivery system's choices as well as the creative. Treat that result as directional unless the setup supports the comparison you intend to make.
documents.s: Two useful variants beat an unplanned matrix

documents.t: Make a 9:16 master for a vertical-feed brief, with enough room to reposition copy for the destination's actual interface. Do not use one fixed “safe zone” for every platform, language, and ad format. As checked on September 5, 2026, TikTok recommends 9:16 for Non-Spark in-feed ads, with a minimum of 540 × 960 pixels. Its safe-zone guidance varies with dimensions, caption length, and additional formats, and it warns that preview and live display can differ. Use the current downloadable templates and verify your specific placement in the TikTok in-feed ad specifications. An editorial delivery target of 1080 × 1920 gives this brief a practical full-HD master; it is not the quoted platform minimum. Confirm accepted encoding, duration, file weight, and account-specific options at upload. For Reels or another placement, use its own current Ads Manager specification and preview rather than assuming TikTok's rules apply. Keep hems, footwear, product names, and the call to action clear of visible controls. Reframe a wide campaign shot if the vertical crop removes the product feature. Make a separate end card for another ratio when necessary; squeezing the whole composition into a smaller box usually weakens legibility.
documents.s: Export for the placement, then inspect its overlays

documents.t: Approve the ad and destination together. The product, color, feature, price, availability, and promotion should agree. If the ad opens on one jacket and lands on an unrelated collection, a low purchase rate may be a destination problem rather than an opening-hook problem. Inspect generated motion for changing prints, logos, fastenings, silhouettes, and accessories. Review the transitions as carefully as the hero frames. A collar cannot disappear before the demonstration removes it, and a bag cannot gain capacity during a packing shot. Have the product owner sign off the merchandise, the creative lead sign off the cut, and the marketer sign off the destination and test setup. Preview the final uploaded file rather than approving only the editing timeline. Compression, player overlays, or a misplaced caption can change what the viewer understands.
documents.s: Review every claim through the landing page

documents.t: Select the primary metric from the campaign objective before launch. For an acquisition test, that might be cost per purchase or purchase conversion under a consistent attribution setting. Set the test budget, duration, and sample requirements from baseline volume and the difference worth detecting. A handful of orders is not a universal stopping rule. Use attention and click measures to investigate the result: Observation Next thing to inspect Weak early retention Whether the opening identifies a relevant product quickly enough Good retention, few destination visits Proposition clarity and the reason to take the next step Many clicks, few purchases Destination match, load time, stock, price, and product information Strong commerce result, high production cost Whether the concept can be repeated economically across products These are diagnostic hypotheses. They do not prove that the hook, page, or price caused the result. Compare metrics using the same definitions and attribution window; a “view” on one platform is not necessarily the same event elsewhere. Keep the full test record, including inconclusive results. Avoid declaring a winner from a single early spike or silently changing the offer midway. If both edits fail, revisit the proposition and destination before commissioning ten more openings.
documents.s: Measure the commercial result, then diagnose the edit

documents.t: Track concept development, source production, all generation attempts, product review, editing, audio, captions, and delivery. Keep media spend separate so you can distinguish an expensive production process from an expensive acquisition channel. For illustration, $600 of production work yielding two approved creative variants is $300 per variant. Cropping those variants into three ratios each gives six files, not six independent creative ideas. Price both the underlying concepts and the additional finishing work explicitly. These are hypothetical inputs, not Astria pricing. A promising concept should survive a second SKU without losing its logic. Reuse the shot structure and editing treatment, but replace the evidence with footage of the actual new product. A removable-collar ad is not a template for a jacket whose collar is fixed. For planning across a collection, connect this record to the AI lookbook workflow. If the open question is which production suite fits the team, the Astria vs Higgsfield comparison covers that buying decision. The ad test should decide the creative question, not serve as an unmeasured comparison of tools.
documents.s: Price a repeatable concept, not a folder of exports

documents.t: Include a clear product opening, evidence for the proposition, a legible next step, and a matching destination. A short sequence can do all four jobs. Choose its duration around the message and placement rather than assuming one length is always best.
documents.s: What should a fashion video ad include?

documents.t: Start with two versions that differ in one defined element, such as the opening hook. Keep the product evidence, offer, destination, and other delivery conditions steady so the result answers a useful question.
documents.s: How many fashion ad variants should a first test use?

documents.t: Reviewed product photos can supply the visual basis for generated motion and an edited ad. Check every shot for garment changes, keep commercial text editable, and use filmed evidence when demonstrating the actual behavior or function of the product.
documents.s: Can AI create fashion video ads from product photos?

documents.t: Reuse the approved source assets, then adapt framing, text, audio, and end cards to each placement. Check the current upload specification and preview overlays. A common vertical ratio does not guarantee that the same layout is safe everywhere.
documents.s: Can the same fashion video run on every social placement?

documents.t: Choose a primary metric that matches the campaign objective, with consistent attribution and a planned sample. For acquisition, commerce outcomes matter more than views alone. Use retention and clicks to diagnose the edit, and retain an inconclusive result when the evidence is insufficient. Explore Astria for fashion and ecommerce.
documents.s: Which metric should decide a fashion video-ad test?

documents.t: Originally published September 2024 by Jayesh Gulani. Reviewed August 2026 — see What changed since 2024 at the end for the current model line-up.
documents.s: Fine-Tuning FLUX.1 on Astria: A Developer's Guide to the API

documents.t: FLUX.1, launched in August 2024 by Black Forest Labs, represents a significant advancement in the field of generative deep learning. This innovative model is designed to push the boundaries of creativity, efficiency, and diversity in media generation, particularly focusing on images and videos. With a mission to develop state-of-the-art generative models, FLUX.1 leverages advanced architectures such as flow matching and Denoising Image Transformer (DIT), similar to the technologies employed in Stable Diffusion 3 (SD3).
documents.s: Introduction to FLUX.1

documents.t: FLUX.1 is built on a robust foundation of 12 billion parameters, allowing it to deliver exceptional image fidelity and controllability. This model excels in generating high-quality images that cater to a wide range of applications, from artistic creations to detailed photorealistic outputs. The architecture combines the strengths of transformer models and diffusion techniques, enabling FLUX.1 to outperform its predecessors, including SDXL and SD1.5, in terms of image quality and prompt adherence.
documents.s: Key Features and Innovations

documents.t: FLUX.1 comes in three distinct variants, each designed for different use cases:
documents.s: Variants of FLUX.1

documents.t: Performance: This is the flagship model, offering state-of-the-art performance with exceptional image quality, detail, and diversity. Access: Available exclusively via API, making it suitable for commercial applications. System Requirements: High system requirements, not suitable for consumer hardware.
documents.s: FLUX.1 [Pro]

documents.t: Purpose: A distilled version intended for non-commercial use, ideal for research and development. Features: Provides similar quality and prompt adherence as the Pro version but is more efficient and can run on consumer hardware. Availability: Open-weight model, downloadable for local use.
documents.s: FLUX.1 [Dev]

documents.t: Speed: Optimized for fast image generation, making it suitable for local development and personal projects. Performance: While it sacrifices some image fidelity for speed, it is designed for quick outputs. License: Released under the Apache 2.0 license, allowing for broader usage. Each variant caters to specific needs, from high-performance commercial applications to efficient local development and rapid prototyping.
documents.s: FLUX.1 [Schnell]

documents.t: Fine-tuning FLUX.1 on Astria is easy: you just need a handful of images to get started.
documents.s: Fine-Tuning FLUX.1 on Astria.ai: Step-by-Step Guide

documents.t: Before you can start fine-tuning FLUX.1, you'll need to generate an API key on Astria.ai. Here's how: 1. Login to Astria.ai: Visit Astria.ai and log in using your Gmail ID. 2. Access the API section: Once logged in, navigate to the API section of your account. 3. Generate the API Key: Click on the 'Generate API Key' button. This will create your unique API key, which you can use for all API requests. 4. $20 Free Credits: Upon generating your API key, you'll receive $20 in credits. These credits can be used to create fine-tunes and generate images using FLUX.1.
documents.s: Generate Your API Key

documents.t: Here, we'll walk you through fine-tuning FLUX.1 using the API, specifically focusing on creating a model that excels at generating human face images. We'll use images of a woman from the free stock photo website, Pexels, to fine-tune our model. Prepare your data: Gather around 8-16 high-resolution images. Upload these images to PostImages to get the image URLs. Ensure that the images are diverse in terms of lighting, angles, and expressions to capture the full range of features you want the model to learn. Initiate fine-tuning: Replace YOUR_API_KEY and YOUR_MODEL_ID with your generated API key and Tune ID. Use the following code to fine-tune FLUX.1 for human faces: import requests from io import BytesIO # Replace with your actual API key API_KEY = 'YOUR_API_KEY' # Function to download images and convert them to binary def download_image(url): response = requests.get(url) if response.status_code == 200: return BytesIO(response.content) else: print(f'Error downloading image: {url}, status code: {response.status_code}') return None # Fine-tune a model using Flux.1 def fine_tune_flux_model(api_key): fine_tune_url = 'https://www.astria.ai/tunes' image_urls = [ 'https://i.postimg.cc/9fThRXgx/pexels-sound-on-3756747.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/dttwHYD1/pexels-sound-on-3756750.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/fysTTSwj/pexels-sound-on-3756752.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/prPRtNZs/pexels-sound-on-3756917.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/fRVZsfcQ/pexels-sound-on-3756944.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/0yhvyKnM/pexels-sound-on-3756962.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/LXKmNgZK/pexels-sound-on-3756993.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/ZqyT8xnx/pexels-sound-on-3760859.jpg', 'https://i.postimg.cc/RF748Cc3/pexels-sound-on-3760918.jpg' ] images = [] for url in image_urls: image = download_image(url) if image: images.append(('tune[images][]', ('image.jpg', image, 'image/jpeg'))) fine_tune_data = { 'tune[class_name]': 'woman', 'tune[name]': 'woman', 'tune[title]': 'Flux Tune Model 1', 'tune[base_fine-tune]': 'Flux.1', 'tune[model_type]': 'lora', 'tune[branch]': 'flux1' } fine_tune_headers = { 'Authorization': f'Bearer {api_key}' } fine_tune_response = requests.post(fine_tune_url, headers=fine_tune_headers, data=fine_tune_data, files=images) if fine_tune_response.status_code == 200: tune_id = fine_tune_response.json()['id'] print(f'Fine-tuning started for tune ID: {tune_id}') return tune_id else: print(f'Error fine-tuning model: {fine_tune_response.status_code}, {fine_tune_response.text}') return None # Main execution flux_tune_id = fine_tune_flux_model(API_KEY) 6. Monitor the progress: Fine-tuning typically takes about 30-60 minutes. You can monitor this through the provided URL. 7. Generate the images: Once fine-tuning is complete, use the following code to generate images: import requests API_KEY = 'YOUR_API_KEY' MODEL_ID = 1504994 # The hardcoded ID for the Flux model # Generate images def generate_images(api_key, model_id): generate_url = f'https://www.astria.ai/tunes/{model_id}/prompts' generate_data = { 'text': '<LoRA:`MODEL_ID`:1.0> sks woman In the style of TOK, a photo editorial avant-garde dramatic action pose of a person wearing 90s round wacky sunglasses pulling glasses down looking forward, in Tokyo with large marble structures and bonsai trees at sunset with a vibrant illustrated jacket surrounded by illustrations of flowers, smoke, flames, ice cream, sparkles, rock and roll', 'num_images': 4, 'model_type' :'lora', 'model': 'flux.1_dev' } generate_headers = { 'Authorization': f'Bearer {api_key}', 'Content-Type': 'application/json' } generate_response = requests.post(generate_url, headers=generate_headers, json=generate_data) if generate_response.status_code == 200: prompt_id = generate_response.json()['id'] image_url = generate_response.json()['image_url'] print(f'Images generated for prompt ID: {prompt_id}') print(f'Image URL: {image_url}') else: print(f'Error generating images: {generate_response.status_code}, {generate_response.text}') # Main execution generate_images(API_KEY, MODEL_ID) # Main execution generate_images(API_KEY, MODEL_ID)
documents.s: Guide to Fine-Tuning Human Faces

documents.t: Prompt 2: A woman dressed in ornate, golden armour, holding a sword, standing on the battlefield at sunrise, with a determined expression. Prompt 3: A woman driving a classic pink convertible with a shiny finish, reminiscent of a Barbie car, cruising down a candy-coloured boulevard lined with palm trees. She's wearing a stylish outfit in shades of pink and pastels, with oversized sunglasses and a bright smile. The scene is set in a whimsical, dreamlike world with cotton candy clouds, glittering starbursts in the sky, and playful details like oversized flowers and butterflies floating around

documents.t: If you have a pet, here’s how you can fine-tune FLUX.1 to generate stunning new images. 1. Collect your data: Use diverse images of a pet, capturing different poses, environments, and expressions. Ensure the images are consistent in quality for the best results. I have used images of a golden retriever from Pexels. 2. The fine-tuning process: Follow the same steps as mentioned above for human faces, upload the images, and define your parameters. After completion, your model will be capable of generating new and fantastic pet images from your prompts.
documents.s: Guide to Fine-Tuning Pet Photographs

documents.t: Prompt 1: A dog wearing cool sunglasses, lounging on a beach towel with the ocean in the background, under a colourful beach umbrella. Prompt 2: A dog dressed in a tuxedo, sitting at a beautifully set dinner table with a candlelit ambience, looking classy and elegant.
documents.s: Example Prompts

documents.t: While SDXL and SD1.5 have been industry standards for a while, FLUX.1's use of flow matching and DIT architecture gives it a distinct edge. Flux.1 has several key advantages over SD1.5 and SDXL:
documents.s: How Flux.1 Compares to SD1.5 and SDXL

documents.t: Flux.1 achieves exceptional image fidelity, detail, and prompt adherence, setting a new standard for text-to-image generation. It adapts to a fitting cartoon drawing style while still adhering to prompts almost every time. Flux.1 successfully adhered to prompts in testing, outperforming the base SD3 model.
documents.s: Image Quality and Prompt Adherence

documents.t: Flux.1 is more versatile than SD1.5, allowing the generation of many images that would be impossible with SD1.5 without specialized LoRAs or ControlNet. It works well for a wide range of use cases, from realistic to cartoon styles.
documents.s: Versatility

documents.t: FLUX.1, especially when fine-tuned, provides a powerful tool for creators and developers. Whether you're looking to generate human portraits, artistic renditions, or even specific pet images, fine-tuning FLUX.1 using Astria's API opens up new possibilities. It is important to remember that Flux image prompting tends to give better outputs with a more narrative-style prompt rather than the traditional comma-separated tags. Also, what’s truly unique about Flux is its ability to render text – not just single words, but entire sentences – with great clarity. This feature alone opens up a universe of possibilities for businesses looking to integrate text into their images.
documents.s: Summary and What’s Next

documents.t: This guide still describes the fine-tuning flow accurately — you upload images, POST a tune, and generate against it — but the model landscape moved on considerably. Read it for the API mechanics, not the model recommendations. The FLUX line advanced. FLUX.1 [Pro], [Dev], and [Schnell] have been joined by newer releases, including FLUX.2 Pro. The branch and model parameters shown below still work; check the current list before hardcoding one. Gemini-branch references removed the training wait. For many use cases you no longer need to train a LoRA at all — a reference can be created instantly from a handful of images and used the same way in prompts. Editing models joined the line-up. Nano Banana and Seedream handle instruction-based edits (background swap, object removal, colour change) that previously required inpainting or a second pass. The credit grant has changed. The $20 figure below reflects a 2024 promotion. Check current pricing for what a new API key includes today. Always discover models programmatically rather than hardcoding a name — see the API reference for the current endpoints and parameters. If you are producing fashion or ecommerce imagery rather than building on the API, the AI fashion photoshoot guide covers the production side of the same platform.

documents.t: Every ecommerce team knows on-model images perform better than flat lays. Every ecommerce team also knows what it costs to produce them for 600 variants, which is why the long tail of most catalogs is still flat lays and ghost mannequins. The short version: the conversion works well, and its quality is decided almost entirely by your source photography — which is the part nobody wants to hear.
